claim: The heterochronic pathway in C. elegans controls a timely juvenile-to-adult (J/A) transition.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, the heterochronic pathway controls a timely juvenile-to-adult (J/A) transition.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational concept of the study.

claim: The heterochronic regulatory cascade culminates in accumulation of the transcription factor LIN-29, which triggers coordinated execution of transition events.
source: This regulatory cascade of conserved proteins and small RNAs culminates in accumulation of the transcription factor LIN-29, which triggers coordinated execution of transition events.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established understanding.

claim: Two LIN-29 isoforms fulfill distinct functions.
source: We report that two LIN-29 isoforms fulfill distinct functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Functional specialization of LIN-29 isoforms is a consequence of distinct isoform expression patterns, not protein sequence.
source: Functional specialization is a consequence of distinct isoform expression patterns, not protein sequence
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that deletion of the N-terminal extension does not affect function (Figure 6).

claim: Distinct LIN-29 dose sensitivities of individual J/A transition events help to ensure their temporal ordering.
source: we propose that distinct LIN-29 dose sensitivities of the individual J/A transition events help to ensure their temporal ordering.
evidence: This is proposed as a hypothesis based on the observed expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: LIN-41 regulates lin-29a expression.
source: We demonstrate that unique isoform expression patterns are generated by the activities of LIN-41 for lin-29a
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi experiments and Western blotting (Figure 9).

claim: HBL-1 regulates lin-29b expression.
source: We demonstrate that unique isoform expression patterns are generated by the activities of LIN-41 for lin-29a, and of HBL-1 for lin-29b
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi experiments showing precocious LIN-29b accumulation upon HBL-1 depletion (Figure 9).

claim: LIN-28 coordinates LIN-29 isoform activity, in part by regulating both hbl-1 and lin-41.
source: whereas the RNA-binding protein LIN-28 coordinates LIN-29 isoform activity, in part by regulating both hbl-1 and lin-41.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing precocious accumulation of both LIN-29 isoforms in lin-28 mutants (Figure 10).

claim: Coordinated transition from juvenile to adult involves branching of a linear pathway to achieve timely control of multiple events.
source: Our findings reveal that coordinated transition from juvenile to adult involves branching of a linear pathway to achieve timely control of multiple events.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the distinct regulation and function of the two LIN-29 isoforms.

claim: J/A transition in mammals is also known as puberty.
source: This is illustrated by the juvenile-to-adult (J/A) transition of animals, in mammals also known as puberty.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: J/A transition involves coordinated morphological changes of sexual organs as well as various other tissues and organs, including skin.
source: J/A transition involves coordinated morphological changes of sexual organs as well as various other tissues and organs, including skin (Lee and Houk, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The molecular mechanisms that control the onset of J/A transition in humans are poorly understood.
source: The molecular mechanisms that control the onset of J/A transition in humans are poorly understood
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The molecular mechanisms controlling J/A transition have been well studied in C. elegans.
source: The molecular mechanisms that control the onset of J/A transition in humans are poorly understood, but have been well studied in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (Faunes and Larraín, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The heterochronic pathway coordinates somatic cell fate programs in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, J/A transition is controlled by a cascade of regulators termed the heterochronic pathway, which coordinates somatic cell fate programs (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Orthologues of heterochronic genes have been implicated in timing the onset of puberty in mammals including humans.
source: Orthologues of heterochronic genes have also been implicated in timing the onset of puberty in mammals including humans (Abreu et al., 2013; Corre et al., 2016; Ong et al., 2009; Perry et al., 2009; Sulem et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2010) (reviewed in Faunes and Larraín, 2016; Moss and Romer-Seibert, 2014)
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to support the claim.

claim: There is evolutionary conservation of the molecular principles of temporal coordination of J/A transition events.
source: indicating an evolutionary conservation of the molecular principles of temporal coordination of J/A transition events.
evidence: This is inferred from the implication of orthologous genes in mammalian puberty.

claim: The C. elegans J/A transition has been particularly well studied in the epidermis.
source: The C. elegans J/A transition has been particularly well studied in the epidermis
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The epidermal J/A transition encompasses four events related to cell fates and molting.
source: The C. elegans J/A transition has been particularly well studied in the epidermis, where it encompasses four events related to cell fates and molting (Ambros, 1989)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Seam cells undergo asymmetric (self-renewal) divisions during larval stages and cease to do so in adult animals.
source: First, skin progenitor cells called seam cells, which undergo asymmetric (self-renewal) divisions during larval stages, cease to do so in adult animals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about seam cell behavior.

claim: The last seam cell division takes place during the transition from the third (L3) to the last (L4) larval stage.
source: The last seam cell division takes place during the transition from the third (L3) to the last (L4) larval stage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the timing of seam cell division.

claim: During the mid-L4 stage, seam cells fuse into a syncytium, a state considered terminally differentiated.
source: Second, during the mid-L4 stage, seam cells fuse into a syncytium, a state considered terminally differentiated (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Animals generate an adult cuticle characterized by the presence of adult-specific collagens and a microscopically visible structure known as adult alae.
source: Third, animals generate an adult cuticle, characterized by the presence of adult-specific collagens (Cox and Hirsh, 1985) and a microscopically visible structure known as adult alae (Singh and Sulston, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Following shedding of the L4 cuticle, animals stop molting.
source: Fourth, following shedding of the L4 cuticle, animals stop molting, the process of cuticle synthesis and shedding that happens at the end of each larval stage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about molting behavior.

claim: Genetic screens have identified precocious and retarded mutations that affect the timing of somatic adult features relative to sexual maturity.
source: Genetic screens have identified precocious and retarded mutations (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984), which cause animals to exhibit somatically adult features before reaching sexual maturity or retain juvenile somatic features after reaching sexual maturity, respectively.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Heterochronic genes regulate the initiation of J/A transition events.
source: Thus, the identified factors, called heterechronic genes, regulate the initiation of J/A transition events.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypes of precocious and retarded mutations.

claim: lin-29 encodes a transcription factor of the EGR/Krüppel family.
source: Among these genes, lin-29, encoding a transcription factor of the EGR/Krüppel family, is considered the downstream-most gene of the heterochronic pathway (Rougvie and Moss, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: lin-29 is considered the downstream-most gene of the heterochronic pathway.
source: Among these genes, lin-29, encoding a transcription factor of the EGR/Krüppel family, is considered the downstream-most gene of the heterochronic pathway (Rougvie and Moss, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: LIN-29 accumulates immediately prior to transition to adulthood during the last (L4) larval stage.
source: Indeed, LIN-29 accumulates immediately prior to transition to adulthood during the last (L4) larval stage (Bettinger et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Current models of the heterochronic pathway depict a simple linear chain of events during the last larval stages that leads to upregulation of LIN-29.
source: Current models of the heterochronic pathway depict a simple linear chain of events during the last larval stages that leads to upregulation of LIN-29 (Faunes and Larraín, 2016; Moss and Romer-Seibert, 2014; Rougvie and Moss, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The miRNA let-7 accumulates during the L3 stage to inhibit synthesis of the RNA binding protein LIN-41.
source: The miRNA let-7 accumulates during the L3 stage to inhibit synthesis of the RNA binding protein LIN-41 (Ding and Großhans, 2009; Reinhart et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: LIN-41 translationally represses lin-29.
source: Since LIN-41 translationally represses lin-29 (Aeschimann et al., 2017), its decreased levels during L4 allow for accumulation of LIN-29.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Decreased LIN-41 levels during L4 allow for accumulation of LIN-29.
source: Since LIN-41 translationally represses lin-29 (Aeschimann et al., 2017), its decreased levels during L4 allow for accumulation of LIN-29.
evidence: This is inferred from the repressive relationship between LIN-41 and lin-29.

claim: All four epidermal J/A events require LIN-29.
source: As all four epidermal J/A events require LIN-29 (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Bettinger et al., 1997), this pathway architecture can ensure their coordinated execution.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The linear pathway architecture can ensure coordinated execution of J/A transition events.
source: As all four epidermal J/A events require LIN-29 (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984; Bettinger et al., 1997), this pathway architecture can ensure their coordinated execution.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of LIN-29 for all four events.

claim: Multiple lines of evidence challenge the simple linear model of the heterochronic pathway.
source: However, multiple lines of evidence challenge this simple linear model.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study.

claim: LIN-29 occurs in two protein isoforms, LIN-29a and LIN-29b.
source: First, LIN-29 occurs in two protein isoforms, LIN-29a and LIN-29b (Rougvie and Ambros, 1995)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: LIN-41 appears to silence only lin-29a but not lin-29b.
source: and LIN-41 appears to silence only lin-29a but not lin-29b (Aeschimann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: lin-41(0) mutant precocious phenotypes are only partially penetrant, unlike the retarded lin-29(0) mutant phenotypes.
source: Second, lin-41(0) mutant precocious phenotypes, unlike the retarded lin-29(0) mutant phenotypes, are only partially penetrant (Slack et al., 2000)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Partial penetrance of lin-41(0) phenotypes indicates additional control of LIN-29 beyond repression by LIN-41.
source: Second, lin-41(0) mutant precocious phenotypes, unlike the retarded lin-29(0) mutant phenotypes, are only partially penetrant (Slack et al., 2000), indicating additional control of LIN-29 beyond repression by LIN-41.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial penetrance of lin-41(0) phenotypes.

claim: let-7 mutations do not recapitulate all phenotypes of lin-29(0).
source: Third, let-7 mutations do not recapitulate all phenotypes of lin-29(0) (Ambros, 1989)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: let-7 appears dispensable for proper timing of seam cell fusion.
source: as let-7 appears dispensable for proper timing of seam cell fusion (Hunter et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: LIN-29a and LIN-29b share most of their protein sequence with the exception of 142 amino acids at the N-terminus that are unique to LIN-29a.
source: LIN-29a and LIN-29b share most of their protein sequence with the exception of 142 amino acids at the N-terminus that are unique to LIN-29a (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that LIN-29 isoforms function redundantly.
source: Previous studies have suggested that these isoforms function redundantly: they share a common co-factor, MAB-10 (Harris and Horvitz, 2011), they have similar expression patterns, and they are interchangeable in complementation analysis (Bettinger et al., 1996; Bettinger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: LIN-29 isoforms share a common co-factor, MAB-10.
source: Previous studies have suggested that these isoforms function redundantly: they share a common co-factor, MAB-10 (Harris and Horvitz, 2011)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: LIN-29 isoforms have similar expression patterns according to previous studies.
source: they have similar expression patterns
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding that is challenged by the current study.

claim: LIN-29 isoforms are interchangeable in complementation analysis.
source: and they are interchangeable in complementation analysis (Bettinger et al., 1996; Bettinger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The lin-29a and lin-29b isoforms differ in function and expression patterns.
source: However, employing isoform-specific mutations and endogenous protein tagging, we show here that the lin-29a and lin-29b isoforms differ in function and expression patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Seam cell fusion relies only on LIN-29b, but not on LIN-29a or MAB-10.
source: The most striking functional difference occurs in seam cell fusion, which relies only on LIN-29b, but not on LIN-29a or MAB-10.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: lin-29a is regulated by LIN-41.
source: Moreover, whereas lin-29a is regulated by LIN-41
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments and Western blotting (Figure 9).

claim: The lin-29b isoform is regulated by the transcription factor HBL-1.
source: the lin-29b isoform is regulated by the transcription factor HBL-1
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments showing precocious LIN-29b accumulation upon HBL-1 depletion (Figure 9).

claim: Regulation by LIN-41 and HBL-1 results in distinct spatiotemporal expression of the two LIN-29 isoforms.
source: which results in a distinct spatiotemporal expression of the two isoforms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging of endogenously tagged LIN-29 isoforms (Figure 7).

claim: The expression patterns alone can explain the unique phenotypic consequences of the isoform-specific mutations.
source: The expression patterns alone can explain the unique phenotypic consequences of the isoform-specific mutations
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that precocious expression of either isoform can induce seam cell fusion (Figure 8).

claim: The sequence difference in the N-terminal portion of the two isoforms does not contribute to functional differences.
source: whereas the sequence difference in the N-terminal portion of the two isoforms does not contribute to functional differences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that deletion of the N-terminal extension does not affect LIN-29a function (Figure 6).

claim: Coordination of the activities of LIN-29a and LIN-29b is achieved through LIN-28.
source: Coordination of the activities of LIN-29a and LIN-29b is achieved through LIN-28, an RNA-binding protein that regulates both HBL-1 and let-7–LIN-41.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing precocious accumulation of both LIN-29 isoforms in lin-28 mutants (Figure 10).

claim: LIN-28 is an RNA-binding protein that regulates both HBL-1 and let-7–LIN-41.
source: Coordination of the activities of LIN-29a and LIN-29b is achieved through LIN-28, an RNA-binding protein that regulates both HBL-1 and let-7–LIN-41.
evidence: This is stated with supporting data from Figure 10 and citations.

claim: The findings help to reframe the regulatory logic that enables the heterochronic pathway to coordinate different events into an overall larval-to-adult transition program.
source: Taken together, our findings help to reframe the regulatory logic that enables the heterochronic pathway to coordinate different events into an overall larval-to-adult transition program.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Seam cells fused normally in 100% of the let-7(xe150) and let-7(n2853) mutant animals.
source: we observed that seam cells fused normally in 100% of the let-7(xe150) and let-7(n2853) mutant animals, confirming that let-7 is indeed dispensable for seam cell fusion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: let-7 is dispensable for seam cell fusion.
source: we observed that seam cells fused normally in 100% of the let-7(xe150) and let-7(n2853) mutant animals, confirming that let-7 is indeed dispensable for seam cell fusion (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: Overexpression of lin-41 had previously been reported to prevent seam cell fusion.
source: Contrasting with the normal seam cell fusion in let-7 mutant animals, overexpression of lin-41 had previously been reported to prevent seam cell fusion (Slack et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: lin-41(xe8[∆LCS]) mutant animals exhibit sustained high LIN-41 levels during the L4 stage.
source: However, when we examined lin-41(xe8[∆LCS]) mutant animals (Figure 1B), which lack the let-7 complementary sites (LCSs) in the lin-41 3'UTR and thus exhibit sustained high LIN-41 levels during the L4 stage (Aeschimann et al., 2017; Ecsedi et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Seam cell fusion occurred normally in lin-41(xe8[∆LCS]) mutant animals.
source: However, when we examined lin-41(xe8[∆LCS]) mutant animals (Figure 1B), which lack the let-7 complementary sites (LCSs) in the lin-41 3'UTR and thus exhibit sustained high LIN-41 levels during the L4 stage (Aeschimann et al., 2017; Ecsedi et al., 2015), seam cell fusion occurred normally.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: The activity of the let-7–LIN-41 module cannot account for all the J/A transition events regulated by lin-29.
source: Hence, the activity of the let-7–LIN-41 module cannot account for all the J/A transition events regulated by lin-29.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that seam cell fusion occurs normally in let-7 and lin-41 mutants but not in lin-29 mutants.

claim: let-7–LIN-41 regulate lin-29a (and mab-10), but presumably not lin-29b.
source: Recently, we showed that let-7–LIN-41 regulate lin-29a (and mab-10), but presumably not lin-29b (Aeschimann et al., 2017; Aeschimann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: In let-7(0) and lin-41(∆LCS) animals, LIN-29a and MAB-10 levels are expected to remain low in the L4 stage while LIN-29b can accumulate.
source: Accordingly, in let-7(0) and lin-41(∆LCS) animals, LIN-29a and MAB-10 levels are expected to remain low in the L4 stage while LIN-29b can accumulate.
evidence: This is inferred from the regulatory relationships between let-7, LIN-41, and the LIN-29 isoforms.

claim: lin-29(xe40) is a lin-29a-specific deletion mutation.
source: We used these, and the previously generated lin-29(xe40) (henceforth lin-29a(∆)) and mab-10(xe44) (henceforth mab-10(0)) mutant strains (Aeschimann et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: mab-10(xe44) is a mab-10 null mutation.
source: We used these, and the previously generated lin-29(xe40) (henceforth lin-29a(∆)) and mab-10(xe44) (henceforth mab-10(0)) mutant strains (Aeschimann et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: MAB-10 is thought not to directly bind to DNA, but to bind to, and modulate the activity of, both LIN-29 isoforms.
source: MAB-10 itself is thought not to directly bind to DNA, but to bind to, and modulate the activity of, both LIN-29 isoforms (Harris and Horvitz, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) single mutant animals showed unperturbed seam cell fusion.
source: lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) single mutant animals, as well as mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) double mutant animals showed unperturbed seam cell fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) double mutant animals showed unperturbed seam cell fusion.
source: lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) single mutant animals, as well as mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) double mutant animals showed unperturbed seam cell fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Unperturbed seam cell fusion in lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) animals is consistent with the functional fusion seen in let-7(0) and lin-41(∆LCS) animals.
source: This is consistent with the functional fusion seen in let-7(0) and lin-41(∆LCS) animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous observations.

claim: Penetrant seam cell fusion defects were observed in both lin-29b(lf) and lin-29b(∆) single mutant strains.
source: In striking contrast to these findings, we observed penetrant seam cell fusion defects in both lin-29b(lf) and lin-29b(∆) single mutant strains
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The seam cell fusion phenotype in lin-29b mutants was not enhanced by concomitant loss of mab-10 expression.
source: and this phenotype was not enhanced by concomitant loss of mab-10 expression, that is in mab-10 lin-29b double mutant animals (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The findings support the notion that the let-7–LIN-41–LIN-29a/MAB-10 module is dispensable for seam cell fusion.
source: These findings support the notion that the let-7–LIN-41–LIN-29a/MAB-10 module is dispensable for seam cell fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that seam cell fusion occurs normally in the absence of these factors.

claim: LIN-29b is both necessary and sufficient for wild-type seam cell fusion.
source: They also reveal an unanticipated specialization of LIN-29 isoforms, with LIN-29b being both necessary and sufficient for wild-type seam cell fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only LIN-29b mutants show seam cell fusion defects and that precocious expression of LIN-29b can induce fusion.

claim: The two LIN-29 isoforms fulfill distinct and non-redundant functions.
source: We conclude that the two LIN-29 isoforms fulfill distinct and non-redundant functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the distinct phenotypes of isoform-specific mutants.

claim: lin-29ab(∆) animals exhibit a fully penetrant phenotype where seam cells do not exit the cell cycle but instead continue to divide.
source: As shown previously (Aeschimann et al., 2019; Ambros and Horvitz, 1984), lin-29ab(∆) (lin-29(xe37)) animals exhibit a fully penetrant phenotype: seam cells do not exit the cell cycle but instead continue to divide so that all animals show at least 25 seam cells instead of the canonical 16 at the young adult stage (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Seam cells exit the cell cycle normally in lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) animals.
source: By contrast, seam cells exit the cell cycle normally in lin-29a(∆) and mab-10(0) animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: A partially penetrant defect in seam cell cycle exit occurs in mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) double mutant animals.
source: A partially penetrant defect occurs in mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) double mutant animals (Figure 3D), recapitulating the phenotype of let-7(n2853) and lin-41(∆LCS) animals (Aeschimann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3D and citations.

claim: Depletion of LIN-29b alone suffices to permit unscheduled seam cell divisions in young adult animals.
source: Unlike loss of LIN-29a alone, depletion of LIN-29b alone suffices to permit unscheduled seam cell divisions in young adult animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: The seam cell cycle exit phenotype is more penetrant in lin-29b(∆) than in lin-29b(lf) animals.
source: The phenotype is more penetrant in lin-29b(∆) than in lin-29b(lf) animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Loss of mab-10 enhances the lin-29b(lf) but not the lin-29b(∆) mutant phenotype for seam cell cycle exit.
source: Moreover, loss of mab-10 enhances the lin-29b(lf) but not the lin-29b(∆) mutant phenotype.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: All three factors, LIN-29a, LIN-29b and MAB-10, are involved in seam cell cell cycle exit.
source: Collectively, these data thus confirm an involvement of all three factors, LIN-29a, LIN-29b and MAB-10 in seam cell cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotypes of various mutant combinations.

claim: LIN-29b has a more prominent role than LIN-29a in seam cell cycle exit.
source: The data also suggest a more prominent role for LIN-29b versus LIN-29a
evidence: This is inferred from the more penetrant phenotype of lin-29b mutants compared to lin-29a mutants.

claim: MAB-10 has a function in promoting LIN-29 activity in seam cell cycle exit.
source: and a function for MAB-10 in promoting LIN-29 activity in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhancement of phenotypes in double mutants lacking MAB-10.

claim: Cell division and terminal differentiation are normally mutually exclusive, tightly coupled events.
source: Cell division and terminal differentiation are normally mutually exclusive, tightly coupled events.
evidence: This is stated as general biological knowledge.

claim: Exit from the cell division cycle is frequently considered a central aspect of terminal cell differentiation.
source: In fact, exit from the cell division cycle is frequently considered a central aspect of terminal cell differentiation (Myster and Duronio, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Nuclear divisions continued to occur after seam cells had fused at the L4 stage in mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) mutant animals.
source: Hence, we were surprised to find that nuclear divisions continued to occur after seam cells had fused at the L4 stage in mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) mutant animals (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Although all seam cells fused in all mab-10(0) lin-29a(∆) animals in the L4 stage, cell junctions were apparent again in the young adult stage.
source: We investigated this apparent discrepancy further and found that although in the L4 stage, all seam cells fused in all animals, cell junctions were apparent again in the young adult stage.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Following unscheduled divisions of seam cell nuclei in syncytia, pairs of seam cell nuclei were separated from other pairs by cell junctions.
source: Specifically, following the unscheduled divisions of seam cell nuclei in these syncytia, pairs of seam cell nuclei were separated from other pairs by cell junctions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Exit from the cell cycle is not elicited by cell fusion.
source: We conclude that exit from the cell cycle is not elicited by cell fusion
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that seam cells can fuse but still undergo cell division.

claim: Cell fusion does not require permanent cell cycle exit.
source: and vice versa, that cell fusion does not require permanent cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that seam cells can fuse but still undergo cell division.

claim: An adult cuticle is characterized by alae, ridges along the lateral sides of the whole worm that are secreted by seam cells.
source: An adult cuticle is characterized by alae (Figure 4A (I)), ridges along the lateral sides of the whole worm that are secreted by seam cells (Singh and Sulston, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: A complete lack of alae was observed in lin-29ab(Δ) young adults.
source: Consistent with previous results (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984), we observed a complete lack of alae in lin-29ab(Δ) young adults (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4B and citations.

claim: lin-29a(∆) mutant animals were partially defective in alae formation, exhibiting weak alae structures.
source: lin-29a(∆) mutant animals were partially defective in alae formation, exhibiting weak alae structures (Figure 4A (II)) that either covered the whole worm ('complete') or at least 50% of the body length ('partial') (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The 'partial alae' phenotype in lin-29a(∆) animals appears to reflect a delay in alae synthesis.
source: The 'partial alae' phenotype appears to reflect a delay in alae synthesis because 4 hr later, all lin-29a(∆) animals had complete, yet still weak, alae (n = 20).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that alae become complete over time.

claim: Animals depleted of LIN-29b either exhibited only alae patches or lacked alae entirely.
source: Animals depleted of LIN-29b either exhibited only alae patches (Figure 4A (III, IV)) or lacked alae entirely (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Complete alae were not observed in lin-29b mutants even 4 hr later.
source: and unlike in the lin-29a(∆) animals, complete alae were not observed even 4 hr later (n = 20).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: lin-29b(Δ) animals had a more penetrant 'no alae' phenotype than lin-29b(lf) mutant animals.
source: lin-29b(Δ) animals had a more penetrant 'no alae' phenotype than lin-29b(lf) mutant animals, with almost half of the former animals lacking any detectable alae structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Neither lin-29b mutation fully recapitulated the lin-29ab(∆) phenotype for alae formation.
source: However, neither lin-29b mutation fully recapitulated the lin-29ab(∆) phenotype
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the phenotypes in Figure 4B.

claim: The alae defects were qualitatively distinct in the lin-29a(∆) and the lin-29b(∆) mutant animals.
source: and the alae defects were qualitatively distinct in the lin-29a(∆) and the lin-29b(∆) mutant animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the different types of alae defects observed in the two mutants.

claim: mab-10 mutant animals displayed normal, wild-type alae formation.
source: Finally, mab-10 mutant animals displayed normal, wild-type alae formation (Harris and Horvitz, 2011)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Absence of MAB-10 did not enhance the phenotypes of any of the lin-29a or lin-29b mutations for alae formation.
source: and absence of MAB-10 did not enhance the phenotypes of any of the lin-29a or lin-29b mutations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Both LIN-29a and LIN-29b, but not MAB-10, are required for wild-type alae formation.
source: We conclude that both LIN-29a and LIN-29b, but not MAB-10, are required for wild-type alae formation
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotypes of various mutant combinations.

claim: The functions of LIN-29a and LIN-29b in alae formation are partially distinct.
source: and that their functions are partially distinct.
evidence: This is inferred from the qualitatively different alae defects in the two mutants.

claim: All lin-29ab(∆) animals exhibited at least one extra molt, with ~50% exhibiting two extra molts.
source: We confirmed a previous report (Ambros and Horvitz, 1984) that lin-29 was required for the exit from the molting cycle by observing that all lin-29ab(∆) animals exhibited at least one extra molt, with ~50% exhibiting two extra molts in the time-frame of the experiment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5B and citations.

claim: Animals with mab-10(0), lin-29a(Δ), lin-29b(lf), lin-29b(Δ) single mutations and mab-10(0) lin-29b(lf) and mab-10(0) lin-29b(Δ) double mutations did not display defects in exiting the molting cycle.
source: By contrast, animals with almost all other single or double mutant combinations, that is mab-10(0), lin-29a(Δ), lin-29b(lf), lin-29b(Δ) single mutations and mab-10(0) lin-29b(lf) and mab-10(0) lin-29b(Δ) double mutations, did not display defects in exiting the molting cycle.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: A small percentage of mab-10(0) lin-29a(Δ) animals executed one or two extra molts.
source: The only exception were mab-10(0) lin-29a(Δ) animals, of which a small percentage executed one or two extra molts.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: LIN-29a and LIN-29b have a redundant function in promoting the exit from the molting cycle.
source: We conclude that LIN-29a and LIN-29b have a redundant function in promoting the exit from the molting cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that loss of either isoform alone does not cause molting defects.

claim: MAB-10 has a minor contribution to exit from the molting cycle that becomes detectable in a sensitized background.
source: Their co-factor MAB-10 has a minor contribution that becomes detectable in a sensitized background.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mab-10(0) lin-29a(Δ) double mutants show a weak molting defect.

claim: The unique N-terminal extension of 142 amino acids of LIN-29a is not responsible for functional specialization.
source: Since our experiments show that LIN-29a and LIN-29b have partially distinct functions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), we asked whether their molecular differences, that is the unique N-terminal extension of 142 amino acids of LIN-29a (Figure 2A), are responsible for functional specialization.
evidence: This is addressed by experiments showing that deletion of the N-terminal extension does not affect function (Figure 6).

claim: Removal of the N-terminus did not affect the spatiotemporal expression pattern of lin-29a.
source: Moreover, the removal of the N-terminus did not affect the spatiotemporal expression pattern of lin-29a, and its expression remained under control of LIN-41 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Deletion of the LIN-29a-specific N-terminus did not compromise LIN-29a function for all four J/A transition events.
source: We characterized the phenotypes of lin-29a(∆N), alone or in combination with a mab-10(0) allele, for all four J/A transition events. In all assays, deletion of the LIN-29a-specific N-terminus did not compromise LIN-29a function, resulting in a wild-type phenotype for all four J/A transition events (Figure 6B–D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The distinct functions of LIN-29a and LIN-29b are not mediated by sequence differences.
source: This data suggests that the distinct functions of LIN-29a and LIN-29b are not mediated by sequence differences, although we cannot formally exclude a contribution of the remaining unique 23 amino acids.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional equivalence of LIN-29a and LIN-29a(ΔN).

claim: lin-29a and lin-29b transcripts were previously reported to exhibit largely similar temporal patterns of accumulation.
source: lin-29a and lin-29b transcripts were previously reported to exhibit largely similar temporal patterns of accumulation, being both detectable from L1 stage on, with increasing levels during development, peaking at the L4 stage, and decreasing in adulthood (Rougvie and Ambros, 1995).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A similar spatiotemporal expression pattern of LIN-29 isoforms was deduced from promoter activity reporter experiments.
source: Furthermore, a similar spatiotemporal expression pattern was deduced from promoter activity reporter experiments (Bettinger et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Transcript quantification and promoter activity measurements do not account for additional layers of post-transcriptional regulation.
source: However, transcript quantification and promoter activity measurements do not account for additional layers of post-transcriptional regulation, such as LIN-41-mediated translational repression of lin-29a (Aeschimann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous studies.

claim: Previous analysis of LIN-29 protein accumulation by immunofluorescence could not distinguish between the two protein isoforms.
source: Previous analysis of LIN-29 protein accumulation by immunofluorescence could not distinguish between the two protein isoforms (Bettinger et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The levels of the LIN-29b protein agreed with its previously reported pattern of mRNA accumulation.
source: The levels of the LIN-29b protein agreed with its previously reported pattern of mRNA accumulation, with detectable accumulation throughout larval stages and an increase in levels in the L3 and L4 stages (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 7A.

claim: LIN-29a protein was undetectable in L1 or L2 stage worms, accumulated weakly in L3 stage, and peaked in L4 stage worms.
source: By contrast, although the lin-29a transcript is detectable in L1 and abundant in L2 (Rougvie and Ambros, 1995), LIN-29a protein was undetectable in L1 or L2 stage worms, accumulated weakly in L3 stage, and peaked in L4 stage worms.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 7A.

claim: The temporal expression pattern of LIN-29a protein is consistent with its post-transcriptional regulation by LIN-41.
source: This is consistent with its post-transcriptional regulation by LIN-41 (Aeschimann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels and the known regulation by LIN-41.

claim: LIN-29b was first detectable in lateral seam cell nuclei of late L3 worms.
source: LIN-29b was first detectable in lateral seam cell nuclei of late L3 worms (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 7B.

claim: In mid-L4 stage animals, LIN-29b also accumulated, weakly, in the major hypodermal syncytium hyp7.
source: Subsequently, in mid-L4 stage animals, it also accumulated, weakly, in the major hypodermal syncytium hyp7 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 7C.

claim: LIN-29a was not detected in either seam cells or the major hypodermal syncytium hyp7 during the L3 stage.
source: By contrast, LIN-29a was not detected in either seam cells or the major hypodermal syncytium hyp7 during the L3 stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 7B.

claim: LIN-29a accumulation began in both seam cells and hyp7 in mid-L4 stage worms.
source: Instead, LIN-29a accumulation began in both cell types in mid-L4 stage worms (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 7C.

claim: Protein levels of both LIN-29a and LIN-29b peaked in lateral seam cells and hyp7 in late L4 stage animals and persisted into adulthood.
source: Finally, protein levels of both LIN-29a and LIN-29b peaked in lateral seam cells and hyp7 in late L4 stage animals and persisted into adulthood (Figure 7D, data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 7D.

claim: lin-29a and lin-29b differ in their spatial as well as temporal expression patterns in the epidermis.
source: Taken together, our detailed analysis shows that lin-29a and lin-29b differ in their spatial as well as temporal expression patterns in the epidermis, likely explaining their distinct function in the four J/A transition events.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the confocal imaging data in Figure 7.

claim: col-10-driven expression of either LIN-29 isoform induced precocious seam cell fusion.
source: Strikingly, col-10-driven expression of either isoform induced precocious seam cell fusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Individual animals with fused seam cells were observed already at 10 hr after plating at 25°C, during the L1 stage.
source: Specifically, we observed individual animals with fused seam cells already at 10 hr after plating at 25°C, that is during the L1 stage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the precocious expression experiments.

claim: At 15 hr after plating, in early L2, all animals had at least partially fused seam cells, with >90% of animals exhibiting complete fusion.
source: At 15 hr after plating, in early L2, all animals had at least partially fused seam cells, with >90% of animals exhibiting complete fusion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Expression of mab-10 from the col-10 promoter did not cause any precocious seam cell fusion.
source: By contrast, expression of mab-10 from the col-10 promoter did not cause any precocious seam cell fusion at this time (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: LIN-29 upregulation alone is sufficient to trigger fusion of seam cells.
source: We conclude that LIN-29 upregulation alone is sufficient to trigger fusion of seam cells
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the precocious fusion experiments.

claim: Upregulation of either LIN-29 isoform suffices to trigger seam cell fusion.
source: and that upregulation of either LIN-29 isoform suffices.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the precocious fusion experiments.

claim: The LIN-29b-specific function observed in seam cell fusion under physiological conditions is not due to sequence differences between the two isoforms, but due to differences in their expression.
source: This data further validates that the LIN-29b-specific function observed in seam cell fusion under physiological conditions (Figure 3A,C) is not due to sequence differences between the two isoforms, but due to differences in their expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the precocious fusion experiments and the N-terminal deletion experiments.

claim: The alae phenotype seen in lin-29b mutant adults corresponds to that seen one stage earlier in precocious lin-41(0) mutant animals.
source: We noticed that the alae phenotype seen in lin-29b mutant adults, small patches of well-formed alae, corresponds to that seen one stage earlier in precocious lin-41(0) mutant animals (Abrahante et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an observation connecting the current findings to previous observations.

claim: The weaker but more continuous alae seen in lin-29a(∆) mutant adults are reminiscent of the appearance of precociously formed alae in HBL-1-depleted L4 stage larvae.
source: By contrast, the weaker but more continuous alae seen in lin-29a(∆) mutant adults are reminiscent of the appearance of precociously formed alae in HBL-1-depleted L4 stage larvae (Abrahante et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an observation connecting the current findings to previous observations.

claim: HBL-1 is a transcription factor of the Hunchback/Ikaros family.
source: Hence, we wondered whether HBL-1, a transcription factor of the Hunchback/Ikaros family (Abrahante et al., 2003; Lin et al., 2003), and LIN-41 might act on distinct lin-29 isoforms.
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: LIN-41 depletion caused precocious accumulation of LIN-29a but not LIN-29b.
source: Consistent with earlier findings (Aeschimann et al., 2017), we found that LIN-41 depletion caused precocious accumulation of LIN-29a but not LIN-29b (Figure 9A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging and Western blot data in Figure 9A,B.

claim: LIN-29a upregulation upon LIN-41 depletion was marked in hyp7 by 20 hr after plating but, with a delay, also occurred in seam cells.
source: This upregulation was marked in hyp7 by 20 hr after plating but, with a delay, also occurred in seam cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Early L3 stage animals exposed to hbl-1 RNAi displayed precocious accumulation of LIN-29b but not LIN-29a.
source: By contrast, early L3 stage animals exposed to hbl-1 RNAi displayed precocious accumulation of LIN-29b but not LIN-29a (Figure 9A,C)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging and Western blot data in Figure 9A,C.

claim: LIN-29b accumulation upon HBL-1 depletion was more pronounced in the lateral seam cells than in hyp7.
source: and this accumulation was more pronounced in the lateral seam cells than in hyp7 (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 9A.

claim: LIN-29b accumulation upon HBL-1 depletion was detectable at the level of the lin-29b transcript.
source: Moreover, it was detectable at the level of the lin-29b transcript (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Precocious accumulation of MAB-10::mCherry was observed in L3 stage animals depleted of LIN-41 in both seam cells and hyp7.
source: Finally, consistent with earlier evidence (Aeschimann et al., 2017), we observed precocious accumulation of a partially functional MAB-10::mCherry protein (Pereira et al., 2019) in L3 stage animals depleted of LIN-41 in both seam cells and hyp7
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 9D and citations.

claim: Depletion of HBL-1 had no effect on MAB-10 accumulation.
source: whereas depletion of HBL-1 had no effect (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 9D.

claim: HBL-1 but not LIN-41 regulates LIN-29b accumulation.
source: We conclude that HBL-1 but not LIN-41 regulates LIN-29b accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments in Figure 9.

claim: MAB-10 and LIN-29a accumulation are regulated by LIN-41 but not by HBL-1.
source: Conversely, MAB-10 and LIN-29a accumulation are regulated by LIN-41 but not by HBL-1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RNAi experiments in Figure 9.

claim: Whether the regulation of LIN-29b by HBL-1 is direct remains to be determined.
source: Whether the regulation of LIN-29b by HBL-1 is direct remains to be determined.
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: The distinct function and regulation of lin-29 isoforms reveals that the heterochronic pathway is not linear but branches into two parallel arms, LIN-41–LIN-29a/MAB-10 and HBL-1–LIN-29b.
source: The distinct function and regulation of lin-29 isoforms that we observed reveals that the heterochronic pathway is not linear but branches into two parallel arms, LIN-41–﻿LIN-29a/MAB-10 and HBL-1–﻿LIN-29b.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the distinct regulation and function of the two isoforms.

claim: lin-41 is the only relevant target of the miRNA let-7.
source: We have previously shown that lin-41 is the only relevant target of the miRNA let-7 (Ecsedi et al., 2015; Aeschimann et al., 2017; Aeschimann et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: let-7 is placed into only one arm of the heterochronic pathway.
source: We have previously shown that lin-41 is the only relevant target of the miRNA let-7 (Ecsedi et al., 2015; Aeschimann et al., 2017; Aeschimann et al., 2019), placing let-7 into only one arm of the pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific regulation of lin-41 by let-7.

claim: lin-28 is the heterochronic gene immediately upstream of let-7.
source: The heterochronic gene immediately upstream of let-7 is lin-28
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: lin-28 directly inhibits let-7 biogenesis.
source: which directly inhibits let-7 biogenesis (Lehrbach et al., 2009; Van Wynsberghe et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: lin-28 was reported to positively regulate hbl-1.
source: Interestingly, lin-28 was also reported to positively regulate hbl-1 (Vadla et al., 2012; Ilbay and Ambros, 2019)
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: lin-28 is a good candidate for being immediately upstream of the pathway's branching point.
source: making it a good candidate for being immediately upstream of the pathway's branching point.
evidence: This is inferred from the dual functions of lin-28 in regulating both let-7 and hbl-1.

claim: Both LIN-29 isoforms accumulate precociously in lin-28 mutant animals.
source: Hence, we analyzed precocious expression of the LIN-29 protein isoforms in a putative null mutant background of lin-28, lin-28(n719), at the early L3 stage. We observed that both isoforms accumulate precociously in lin-28 mutant animals (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: LIN-29 accumulation in lin-28 mutants is initially particularly strong in the seam but over time also increases in hyp7.
source: Accumulation is initially particularly strong in the seam but over time, and in particular for LIN-29a, also increases in hyp7.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 10 and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: lin-29b but not lin-29a mRNA levels are increased in lin-28(n719) mutant relative to wild-type animals.
source: Consistent with acting mainly through HBL-1 and LIN-41, respectively, lin-29b but not lin-29a mRNA levels are increased in lin-28(n719) mutant relative to wild-type animals (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 10B,C.

claim: After 22 hr, when LIN-28 is also repressed in wild-type animals, comparable lin-29b mRNA levels result.
source: After 22 hr, when LIN-28 is also repressed in wild-type animals, comparable lin-29b mRNA levels result.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 10C.

claim: The data support the hypothesis that heterochronic pathway bifurcation occurs downstream of lin-28.
source: Hence, these data support our hypothesis that heterochronic pathway bifurcation occurs downstream of lin-28.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the precocious accumulation of both LIN-29 isoforms in lin-28 mutants.

claim: The temporal order of the individual epidermal J/A transition events is driven by differences in their LIN-29 dose sensitivity and the spatiotemporal differences in lin-29 isoform expression.
source: We propose that, in the unperturbed system, the temporal order of the individual epidermal J/A transition events is driven by differences in their LIN-29 dose sensitivity and the spatiotemporal differences in lin-29 isoform expression (Figure 11A and B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observed expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: Seam cell fusion relies on LIN-29 accumulation in only the seam.
source: Specifically, we hypothesize that seam cell fusion rely on LIN-29 accumulation in only the seam, explaining its early occurrence and dependence on only LIN-29b, which accumulates early in this tissue.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: Accumulation of LIN-29b alone appears insufficient to drive cessation of seam cell division cycles.
source: By contrast, accumulation of LIN-29b alone appears insufficient to drive cessation of seam cell division cycles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that lin-29b mutants show cell cycle defects.

claim: It is unclear when seam cells exit the cell cycle.
source: Although the last seam cell division normally happens at the L3-to-L4 molt, it is unclear when these cells exit the cell cycle (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is stated as an open question.

claim: LIN-29a and LIN-29b can, individually, and more extensively jointly, delay division, but terminating it requires full LIN-29 activity, and thus MAB-10.
source: In fact, our data suggest the possibility of a gradual effect where LIN-29a and LIN-29b can, individually, and more extensively jointly, delay division, that is slow down the cell cycle, but where terminating it requires full LIN-29 activity, and thus MAB-10.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the phenotypes of various mutant combinations.

claim: Exit from the mitotic cycle is the only epidermal J/A transition event for which a defect was observed in mab-10(0) single mutant animals.
source: Consistent with this notion, exit from the mitotic cycle is the only epidermal J/A transition event for which we observed a defect in mab-10(0) single mutant animals
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The additional divisions in mab-10(0) single mutant animals occurred much later than in the other mutant combinations.
source: but the additional divisions occurred much later than in the other mutant combinations (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: Others reported extra molts in, mostly older and male, mab-10 mutant animals.
source: We note that others reported also extra molts in, mostly older and male, mab-10 mutant animals (Harris and Horvitz, 2011), which we did not investigate.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the absence of MAB-10, LIN-29a and/or LIN-29b may suffice to delay the occurrence of the next molt rather than to prevent it entirely.
source: An interesting possibility is that, akin to seam cell division, in the absence of MAB-10, LIN-29a and/or LIN-29b may suffice to delay the occurrence of the next molt rather than to prevent it entirely, and in all animals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the phenotypes.

claim: Both LIN-29 isoforms (but not MAB-10) are required for wild-type alae formation, but their individual loss causes qualitatively different defects.
source: Finally, although both isoforms (but not MAB-10) are required for wild-type alae formation, their individual loss causes qualitatively different defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the alae phenotypes in Figure 4.

claim: The qualitatively different alae defects may reflect an involvement of hyp7, in addition to seam cells, in alae formation.
source: We speculate that this may reflect an involvement of hyp7, in addition to seam cells, in alae formation, either directly or through an effect on seam cells that remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the phenotypes.

claim: MAB-10 function is not required for wild-type alae formation, but enhances precocious alae formation in lin-41 mutant animals.
source: The fact that MAB-10 function is not required for wild-type alae formation, but enhances precocious alae formation in lin-41 mutant animals (Harris and Horvitz, 2011)
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: MAB-10 has a generic function in boosting LIN-29 activity, rather than a specific effect on a subset of LIN-29-regulated targets required for only certain processes.
source: is then in agreement with the idea that it has a generic function in boosting LIN-29 activity, rather than a specific effect on a subset of LIN-29-regulated targets required for only certain processes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the phenotypes.

claim: Genome-wide identification of the targets of the lin-29 isoforms and mab-10 will allow further testing of the notion that MAB-10 has a generic function in boosting LIN-29 activity.
source: We propose that genome-wide identification of the targets of the lin-29 isoforms and mab-10 will allow further testing of this notion in the future.
evidence: This is a proposal for future research.
